problem_summary.summary: Return an index of any value that is strictly greater than its adjacent values, treating values beyond either array end as negative infinity.
problem_summary.input_output: Input: a nonempty integer array with unequal adjacent elements. Return the index of any peak.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for every valid adjacent pair
The required algorithm runs in O(log n) time

brute_force.explanation: Scan indices and test each value against its existing neighbors, treating a missing neighbor at an array boundary as negative infinity. Return the first peak found.
brute_force.correctness_idea: An index is a peak exactly when it is larger than each in-bounds neighbor (the missing boundary neighbor is smaller by definition). The scan checks that condition directly, and the problem guarantees at least one peak.

optimized.explanation: Binary search using the slope between mid and mid + 1. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], a peak exists to the right; otherwise a peak exists at mid or to its left. Shrink until one index remains.
optimized.correctness_idea: Moving toward a larger adjacent value preserves a route to a peak: the chosen interval has a rising boundary on its left and the conceptual negative-infinity boundary on its right. Thus the interval always contains a peak, and its final single index is one.
optimized.time_complexity: O(log n), where n is nums.length.

steps.condition: 9 > 7, so the slope descends to the right; a peak lies at mid or to its left.
5 < 9, so the slope rises rightward and a peak lies to the right.

edge_cases.handling: Index 0 is a peak because both outside neighbors are treated as negative infinity.

edge_cases.case: Peak at the left or right boundary
edge_cases.handling: The corresponding missing neighbor satisfies the peak condition by definition.
The binary search may return any one of them.
Excluded by the constraints; the slope decision depends on this guarantee.
